as_told: A company was so worried about malware on USB sticks that it filled the USB ports of its computers with epoxy glue. The story is told as an example of crude but effective physical security.
lesson: Physically blocking USB ports is a cheap and effective defence against attacks that come through USB devices.
what_happened: Reports from 2005 to 2008 describe organisations that glued or epoxied USB ports, but the records name the reason as stopping data from leaving on portable drives, not malware. The best record is a 2007 FedTech article in which Los Alamos National Laboratory spokesman Kevin Roark says the lab blocked unneeded ports "using hardware, software and epoxy" after a contractor took classified documents home on USB drives in 2006. A 2005 GCN article reports a vendor's claim that an unnamed US "three-letter agency" blocked ports with glue. I found no first-hand record of a company that used epoxy against malware; the lesson about physical port blocking does not depend on who did it or on which threat they feared.

earliest_telling.who: William Jackson, reporting a claim by Aubin of SecureWave
earliest_telling.quote: the agency resorted to physically blocking the ports with glue

original.what: Interview quote from the Los Alamos National Laboratory spokesman on how the lab disabled USB ports after the 2006 classified data incident
original.who: Kevin Roark, Los Alamos National Laboratory spokesman, quoted by Daniel Tynan in FedTech Magazine, "Closed-Door Policy"
original.quote: then blocked them using hardware, software and epoxy

original.what: Earlier report on the same Los Alamos measures; Roark's quoted words here do not name glue or epoxy
original.who: John Zyskowski, GCN, "Thumb drives are too often the victims of convenience"
original.quote: That is the option Los Alamos officials chose with some of the lab's computers in the wake of the recent data security incident, said Kevin Roark, a lab spokesman.

lesson_verdict.why: A controlled field study found that people picked up and plugged in an estimated 45-98% of USB drives dropped on a university campus, so USB devices are a real attack path. NIST guidance (SP 1334) lists epoxy as one way to disable unneeded ports, but I found no study that measures how well physical port blocking reduces attacks.

source.what: Tischer, Durumeric, Foster, Duan, Mori, Bursztein and Bailey, "Users Really Do Plug in USB Drives They Find", IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy, 2016

search_steps: Open Library full-text search for "USB ports" epoxy: only hobby and repair books; one 2015 book on school computers (Securing the Connected Classroom) mentions pouring epoxy into ports, later than the sources below.

Web searches for companies or agencies that filled USB ports with epoxy: found GCN (2005, 2006), eWeek (2006), FedTech (2007, 2017), a Microsoft blog (2008), Dark Reading and CIO articles, and 2014 BadUSB coverage.

Saved GCN 2005 'Pulling the plug' (16 June 2005): a vendor, Aubin of SecureWave, says an unnamed 'three-letter agency' blocked ports with glue. This is a relayed claim and the earliest telling I found.
Saved GCN 2006 (14 December 2006): lists glue as one option and says Los Alamos chose to block ports, but Roark's own quoted words say 'disconnecting or blocking or otherwise disabling', not glue.

FedTech 2007, CIO and Dark Reading returned 403 to direct download; fetched FedTech 'Closed-Door Policy' (dated 2007-09-10) from the Wayback Machine. It quotes Roark saying the lab blocked ports 'using hardware, software and epoxy'. CIO and Dark Reading were not saved.

Saved a Microsoft e-discovery blog post (2008-09-08): the author writes that he once knew a sysadmin who 'put epoxy into the USB ports of all new laptops that came into his organization'. This is second-hand and gives data leakage as the reason.
Tried a Slashdot story from 3 March 2006 on the topic: the mirror returned a bot check and the Wayback copy was not found.
Every saved source gives data theft or leakage as the reason. I found no first-hand record that names malware as the reason for epoxy in ports.
Lesson: saved Tischer et al. 2016 (USB drop study) and NIST SP 1334 (portable media in OT), which lists 'port locks, epoxy, locking cabinets' as physical ways to disable ports.
Tried the SecurityInfoWatch article 'Portable Data Storage Devices: Security Nightmare' (mentions filling ports with plastic resin); it returned 403 and I could not check its date.
English Wikipedia search (API) for USB ports, epoxy and glue: no article on the story.
confidence_note: The story is generic and names no company. The records show a government laboratory and an unnamed agency, and they give stopping data theft as the reason, not malware; I class it 'true' because the lesson needs only that an organisation filled ports with epoxy for security. The Los Alamos quote is a spokesman's interview words published by a magazine. The 'super glue' detail in FedTech is the reporter's words, not Roark's.
